summary: Shell sort is insertion sort with a head start: it first sorts elements that are far apart, using a shrinking gap, so small values travel long distances quickly. When the gap reaches 1 the array is nearly sorted and the final insertion-sort pass is cheap.

sections.heading: Idea
sections.body: Plain insertion sort moves an element one position per swap, so a small value near the end takes O(n) steps. Shell sort sorts every h-th element for a decreasing sequence of gaps h, ending with h = 1. An array that is h-sorted stays h-sorted after being k-sorted, so earlier passes are never undone.

sections.heading: Algorithm
bullets: Choose a gap sequence, e.g. n/2, n/4, ..., 1.
For each gap, do an insertion sort on the elements gap apart.
Finish with gap = 1, a normal insertion sort on a nearly sorted array.

sections.heading: Gap sequences
bullets: Shell's original n/2, n/4, ...: simple, worst case O(n²).
Sedgewick's and Ciura's sequences: better in practice (Ciura: 1, 4, 10, 23, 57, 132, 301, 701).

sections.heading: Complexity
bullets: Depends on the gap sequence: from about O(n^1.25) to O(n^1.5) typical, O(n²) worst for poor gaps.
Best case near O(n log n) for already sorted data.

sections.body: With gap 4, compare positions (0,4), (1,5), ... and swap out-of-order pairs; with gap 2 the array is closer to sorted; with gap 1 a final insertion pass finishes with few shifts.

Large-gap passes remove many inversions at once (each swap fixes several), so the final pass sees few inversions and is near O(n). That is why Shell sort is far faster than insertion sort on mid-sized random data.
It needs no recursion or extra memory and is short to implement, so it appears in embedded code and libraries such as uClibc's qsort. Large systems prefer O(n log n) sorts.
The best possible gap sequence is still unknown; analyses give bounds for specific sequences, and Ciura's was found by experiment.

bullets: Insertion sort with gap 1 is a special case.
Comb sort applies the same idea to bubble sort.

takeaways: Insertion sort over elements a gap apart, shrinking the gap to 1.
Complexity depends on the gap sequence; Knuth/Ciura beat n/2.
In place, not stable, short code.
